item.title: Engineered two-photon dissipative confinement of a Kerr-cat qubit using SISIS quantum circuit refrigerator
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Superconductor–insulator–superconductor–insulator–superconductor (SISIS) quantum circuit refrigerator selectively activates two-photon absorption near eV/h≃82.8 GHz, cooling dephasing-induced leakage states back into Kerr parametric oscillator qubit subspace while avoiding single-photon parity-flipping errors.

Grade 0.493 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “Charge-insensitive qubit design derived from the Cooper pair box” · Shumpei Masuda, Tsuyoshi Yamamoto, Shuji Nakamura, Daichi Sugiyama, Akiyoshi Tomonaga

Figure

Excited leakage state populations (A) and qubit state population (B) over time under dephasing and loss. SISIS QCR suppresses leakage nearly as effectively as SINIS while maintaining much higher logical state population against phase flips.

Asks

Can a quantum circuit refrigerator suppress pure-dephasing leakage in Kerr-cat qubits without driving parity-changing single-photon phase-flip errors?

Before

SINIS-based QCR suppresses dephasing leakage via single-photon absorption but broad normal-metal density of states accelerates intra-qubit phase-flip errors.

But

Theoretical and numerical simulation; assumes second-order perturbative Born–Markov coupling, zero magnetic field, and specific Dynes subgap density of states parameter γD.

Tools

SISIS junction QCR · Kerr parametric oscillator (KPO) · Born–Markov master equation · quasiparticle tunneling rate via Fermi's golden rule

Abstract

Kerr-cat qubits realized in periodically driven superconducting nonlinear resonators are a promising platform for quantum information processing with biased noise. Pure dephasing in such systems induces leakage out of the qubit subspace, motivating the use of quantum circuit refrigeration (QCR) to remove excess excitations. While conventional superconductor--insulator--normal-metal--insulator--superconductor (SINIS)-based QCRs can suppress leakage via single-photon absorption, they also enhance QCR-induced phase-flip errors. Here we investigate a QCR based on a superconductor--insulator--superconductor--insulator--superconductor (SISIS) junction coupled to a Kerr parametric oscillator (KPO). We show that a SISIS-based QCR can operate in a regime where single-photon processes are suppressed while two-photon absorption dominates. As a result, the proposed SISIS-based QCR achieves strong suppression of dephasing-induced leakage while substantially reducing the increase in phase-flip errors associated with QCR operation. These results demonstrate that the proposed SISIS-based QCR provides an effective approach for mitigating leakage while limiting QCR-induced phase-flip errors in Kerr-cat qubits.

item.title: One-clean-qubit spectroscopy of simulated Kitaev chains
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Extracts full 2N eigenenergies of an N-site transverse-field Ising model and the N single-particle energies of its mapped Kitaev chain via stroboscopic DQC1 readout on a single control spin.

Grade 0.459 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Semiconductor spin qubits” · Z. M. McIntyre, Daniel Loss

Figure

Stroboscopic control-qubit expectation value vs time, showing resolution of single-particle Kitaev spectrum across trivial and topological regimes under 1/f noise.

Asks

How can the full spectrum and topological crossover of a simulated Kitaev chain be extracted in quantum-dot spin qubit arrays lacking multi-qubit simultaneous readout?

But

Requires simulation time Ttot>2π/δϵmin⁡ and gate infidelity εgate<min⁡[1/(N(J+h)Ttot),δϵmin⁡2/(Nh2)]; demonstrated numerically for N=6.

Tools

Digital-analog quantum simulation · One-clean-qubit (DQC1) model · Jordan-Wigner transformation · Repetition-code control qubit · Drive-engineered Floquet Hamiltonian

Abstract

Spin qubits in gate-defined quantum dots provide a highly programmable platform for simulating condensed-matter phenomena. In this work, we introduce a digital-analog quantum simulation protocol for extracting the single-particle spectrum of a Kitaev chain. The Kitaev chain is mapped onto qubits via the standard Jordan-Wigner transformation and implemented as a drive-engineered, N-site transverse-field Ising model (TFIM) in a linear array of quantum dots. We show that periodically toggling the analog-simulation parameters conditioned on the state of a control qubit causes the dynamics of this control qubit to stroboscopically match the output of the one-clean-qubit (DQC1) model of computation, thereby yielding the full spectrum of the TFIM from measurements of a single spin. Classical postprocessing can then be used to isolate the N single-particle energies of the Kitaev chain from the 2^N eigenenergies of the TFIM. By varying the strength of the Rabi drive used to engineer the synthetic transverse field, the spectral signature of the crossover from the trivial to the topological regime of the Kitaev chain could then be mapped out with measurements of just one spin.

item.title: Programmable CMOS DAC Operating in Cryogenic Environments for Controlling Superconducting Qubits
item.description:
Long shot new result — Fabricated current-based DAC in 90 nm planar CMOS operating at cryogenic temperatures. Enables digital control of output current pulse amplitude, rise/fall slopes, and trigger-controlled pulse width while driving superconducting circuits.

Grade 0.441 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “scaling up: crossbar addressing, cryo-CMOS control, qubit interconnects” · A. Pelteku, D. Reitz, M. Covington, A. Frederick, H. Adebayo, K. D. Hillaire, N. Mitran, Z. Steffen, R. Schwartz, Z. Stegen, J. X. Przybysz, J. Yager, C. Walter, T. Graves, D. Meyer, J. Clark, G. R. Boyd, A. Pesetski

Asks

Can a digitally tunable CMOS current DAC operate at cryogenic temperatures to control flux coupled to superconducting qubits and circuit readout?

But

90 nm planar CMOS technology node.

Tools

90 nm planar CMOS process · Current-based DAC · Cryogenic measurement setup

Abstract

This paper presents the design and test results of a CMOS current-based Digital to Analog Converter (DAC) that operates at cryogenic temperatures and that can be used to precisely control the amount of flux coupled to qubits or that can be used in the readout of superconducting circuits. The current pulse output can be controlled in terms of its amplitude, rise and fall slopes, via digital controls, and pulse width, via external triggers, while driving a superconducting circuit. The design has been implemented in a planar 90 nm CMOS process and test results closely match circuit predictions. The solution's wide degree of digital tunability affords potential application of the same device to many types of quantum circuits, beyond those discussed here. Due to the wide-ranging flexibility of digital CMOS control, we envision that this DAC design will enable the next generation of high-fidelity cryo-CMOS control architectures for superconducting qubits.
